problem:
Harbour Energy collects monthly bills by SEPA Direct Debit, and a new analyst on the team cannot explain who does what when a collection fails. The creditor's billing system sends a file, the money moves, and sometimes it comes back, but the analyst cannot say which party is responsible for the mandate, which party checks the account, which party moves the funds between banks, or who the customer should call when a collection is wrong. The confusion matters because a recent failure was passed between four teams for two weeks: the creditor blamed its bank, the creditor's bank blamed the clearing system, the clearing system pointed to the debtor's bank, and the debtor's bank said the mandate was the creditor's problem. Each party was partly right, and nobody owned the end-to-end outcome.

The four-corner model gives each party a defined corner and a defined responsibility. The creditor owns the mandate, the pre-notification and the collection instruction. The creditor PSP receives the collection, validates it and submits it into the clearing system. The clearing and settlement mechanism moves the collection between the banks and settles the interbank positions. The debtor PSP receives the collection, checks the debtor account and debits it on the due date, and the debtor is the account holder whose funds are collected. A failure at any corner has a different owner, a different message and a different remedy, and the analyst must be able to map each failure to its corner.

The learning goal is practical: given a failed or disputed collection, the learner should be able to name the corner where it failed, the message that carried it there, and the party that must act. Without that map, every exception becomes a round of blame between teams that each see only their own corner.
solution:
Teach and document the model as a responsibility map, not as a diagram to memorise. For each corner, record who the party is, what they own, which message they send and receive, and what they must do when something fails. The creditor owns the mandate, the pre-notification, the collection instruction and the billing generation, and must be able to prove the mandate and the notice. The creditor PSP owns intake validation, submission timing and the interbank message, and must check the mandate reference and the collection details before submitting. The clearing and settlement mechanism owns routing between PSPs and interbank settlement, and must be able to show whether a collection was delivered and settled. The debtor PSP owns the debtor account check, the debit on the due date and the return or refund handling, and the debtor owns the mandate consent and the right to dispute.

Apply the map to every exception type. A missing mandate is a creditor-corner failure. A late submission is a creditor PSP failure. A collection that never arrives is a clearing question. A debit from a closed account is a debtor PSP return. A duplicate is usually a creditor-corner generation failure, and the proof is in the file and the instruction references. For each type, define the evidence that proves the corner, the message that carries the instruction, and the remedy that belongs to that corner.

Finally, make the model operational. Every collection must carry references that survive all four corners, so an investigation can follow one identifier from billing to ledger. The Operations runbook should start every investigation with the same question: which corner, which message, which reference, and which party owns the next action. Review the map whenever a new exception type appears, and add it to the runbook with its corner and remedy.

decision.question: You are the business analyst for Harbour Energy. A customer's direct debit collection was debited twice in one month. The customer complains to Harbour Energy. The billing team blames the creditor PSP, the PSP blames the clearing system, and the debtor PSP says it only followed the instruction it received. You must decide where to start the investigation.

options.label: A
options.detail: Tell the customer to ask their bank for a refund and close the case.

options.label: B
options.detail: Trace the collection from the creditor corner: check the mandate, the billing generation and the file sent to the creditor PSP, then follow the instruction through each corner with its references.

options.label: C
options.detail: Ask the clearing system to reverse both collections immediately.

options.label: D
options.detail: Assume the debtor PSP debited twice and demand it fixes the account.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because the four-corner model makes the creditor corner the starting point: the duplicate was most likely generated in billing or in the file, and tracing the instruction reference through each corner identifies where the second collection entered. Option C asks the clearing system to fix a problem it did not create. Option A hands the customer to another party without establishing the facts. Option D blames the debtor PSP before any evidence shows it created the duplicate.

steps.title: Signs the mandate authorising Harbour Energy to collect
Sends the pre-notification and generates the collection instruction
Validates the collection and submits it to the clearing system
Routes the collection to the debtor PSP and settles the interbank position
Checks the debtor account and debits it on the due date
Returns a status or a return where the debit cannot be made
Routes the return or status back to the creditor PSP
Receives the outcome, reconciles it and notifies or follows up with the debtor as needed
steps.note: Creditor PSP platform and billing system

happy: The debtor signs a mandate, the creditor sends the pre-notification and generates a valid collection, the creditor PSP validates and submits it, the clearing system routes and settles it, and the debtor PSP debits the account on the due date. Each corner performs its own responsibility, the references survive the whole path, and the collection reconciles at the creditor.

negative.title: Mandate missing at the creditor corner
negative.detail: The creditor generates a collection with no valid mandate. The creditor PSP validation should block it, and the creditor must obtain or repair the mandate. The debtor PSP is not the owner of this failure.

negative.title: Collection never reaches the debtor PSP
negative.detail: The collection is lost or delayed between the creditor PSP and the clearing system. Trace the instruction reference through the creditor PSP submission log and the clearing receipt, and resubmit or investigate from the corner where the trail stops.

negative.title: Debtor account cannot be debited
negative.detail: The account is closed or has insufficient funds on the due date. The debtor PSP returns the collection with the applicable reason code, the creditor PSP routes the return to the creditor, and the creditor follows up with the debtor.

negative.title: Duplicate collection from the creditor corner
negative.detail: Billing generates the same collection twice. Identify the duplicate by instruction reference at the creditor PSP, block the second submission, and reverse or refund the duplicate debit under the applicable process if it already settled.

technical: Carry a single end-to-end reference and the mandate reference through all four corners, so any party can trace a collection from billing to ledger. Each corner must log its own receipt, validation result, submission and settlement events with timestamps, so the trail shows where the instruction stopped. Keep the mandate data with the creditor and the account data with the debtor PSP, and pass only the data each corner needs in the interbank message. Use the scheme's status and return messages to communicate outcomes between corners rather than informal emails. Design the investigation view to show all four corners for one collection on a single screen, with the status at each corner.

messages.title: Creditor to creditor PSP collection file, from the creditor corner to its PSP
Interbank direct debit collection from creditor PSP through the clearing system to the debtor PSP
Payment status report between PSPs for acceptance or rejection
Payment return from the debtor PSP for a collection that cannot be debited

fields.tag: Original instruction identification and return reason code
fields.name: Original instruction identification and return reason code

accounting: Each corner posts its own accounting: the creditor PSP credits the creditor on settlement and the debtor PSP debits the debtor on the due date, with the clearing system settling the interbank positions between them. A return reverses the flow as a separate linked event at the corner that initiates it, so the original collection is never deleted. Operations at each corner works from its own worklist, but an end-to-end investigation needs the shared references to connect them. Reconciliation at the creditor matches collections, settlements and returns by instruction reference, and any collection that is missing from the clearing settlement is escalated as a break with the corner identified.

scenarios.given: a collection generated by the creditor
scenarios.when: it is submitted to the creditor PSP
scenarios.then: the creditor PSP validates the mandate reference before sending it to the clearing system

scenarios.given: a collection that the debtor PSP cannot debit
scenarios.then: the return is routed through the clearing system to the creditor PSP with the applicable reason code

scenarios.given: a duplicate collection generated in billing
scenarios.when: the second instruction reaches the creditor PSP
scenarios.then: it is identified by its instruction reference and blocked from submission
the trail shows the status at each of the four corners under one end-to-end reference

questions.explanation: The clearing system moves the collection between the creditor PSP and the debtor PSP and settles the interbank positions. It does not own the mandate or the customer accounts.
options: Routing the collection between PSPs and settling the interbank positions

options: At the creditor corner, checking billing generation and the file sent to the creditor PSP
By asking the customer to prove it
